resources.title: Systematic analysis of 32,111 AI model cards characterizes documentation practice in AI
Interactive Model Cards: A Human-Centered Approach to Model Documentation
resources.abstract: Deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly adopted and deployed by analysts without formal training in NLP or machine learning (ML). However, the documentation intended to convey the model’s details and appropriate use is tailored primarily to individuals with ML or NLP expertise. To address this gap, we conduct a design inquiry into interactive model cards, which augment traditionally static model cards with affordances for exploring model documentation and interacting with the models themselves. Our investigation consists of an initial conceptual study with experts in ML, NLP, and AI Ethics, followed by a separate evaluative study with non-expert analysts who use ML models in their work. Using a semi-structured interview format coupled with a think-aloud protocol, we collected feedback from a total of 30 participants who engaged with different versions of standard and interactive model cards. Through a thematic analysis of the collected data, we identified several conceptual dimensions that summarize the strengths and limitations of standard and interactive model cards, including: stakeholders; design; guidance; understandability & interpretability; sensemaking & skepticism; and trust & safety. Our findings demonstrate the importance of carefully considered design and interactivity for orienting and supporting non-expert analysts using deep learning models, along with a need for consideration of broader sociotechnical contexts and organizational dynamics. We have also identified design elements, such as language, visual cues, and warnings, among others, that support interactivity and make non-interactive content accessible. We summarize our findings as design guidelines and discuss their implications for a human-centered approach towards AI/ML documentation.

The lending model's card reports the selected group-comparison metrics and their assessment scope, without asserting equitable decisions from documentation alone.
The system's card records the stated training context, evaluation procedures and ethical considerations for inspection.

techniques.name: Datasheets for Datasets
techniques.description: A datasheet for a dataset is a short document that accompanies the dataset and answers a set of questions about it, in the way an electronic component comes with a datasheet. Gebru and colleagues group the questions into seven sections: why the dataset was made, what it contains, how it was collected, how it was cleaned and labelled, what it should and should not be used for, how it is distributed, and who maintains it. Creators read the questions before collecting data, answer them when the dataset is finished, and update the sheet when the dataset changes. People considering the dataset read it to judge whether it suits their task and what risks it carries. The questions are a prompt rather than a checklist, and a datasheet records what is known without testing it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model risk team asks a vendor for the datasheet of a transaction dataset before approving it for fraud-model training. The answers on how transactions were sampled, which merchants and periods are missing, and what the data should not be used for let the team judge whether the dataset fits its purpose.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

A hospital trust's data governance group will not release a medical imaging dataset to model developers until its datasheet is complete. The sheet records consent, anonymisation, sensitive attributes and sharing limits, and the group files it with the release approval as the record of what was checked.

A recruitment-technology team documents its CV dataset: the mix of applicants by job category and demographic group, how outcome labels were assigned, and which groups are thinly represented. Developers read this before training a screening model, so they know the limits of the data before they choose and test the model.

limitations.description: Writing a thorough datasheet takes time and knowledge of how the dataset was built, and the work recurs with each version, which can delay release. Gebru et al. note that the overhead is real and that organisational workflows and incentives need to change to accommodate it.

A datasheet describes the dataset as it was when written. Cleaning, augmentation or new data make it wrong unless it is revised, and Gebru et al. say the format fits dynamic datasets poorly, so each updated version needs an updated datasheet.

There is no single mandated template. Gebru et al. give a set of questions and say it is not prescriptive. ECMA-424 (CycloneDX 1.7, December 2025) standardises a machine-readable record of a dataset's contents, sensitive data and owners, but not the account of motivation, collection and intended use. Without enforcement, depth and completeness vary.

Answers come from the dataset's creators and nothing checks them. Creators may leave out sensitive details about collection, consent or bias to avoid legal or commercial exposure, so a datasheet can look complete and still mislead.

A datasheet records what its authors know. It does not measure bias, check coverage or find errors, and Gebru et al. note that spotting societal bias often needs demographic labels that creators may not hold. A clean-looking datasheet is not evidence the data suits a particular use.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.abstract: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains. To address this gap, we propose datasheets for datasets. In the electronics industry, every component, no matter how simple or complex, is accompanied with a datasheet that describes its operating characteristics, test results, recommended uses, and other information. By analogy, we propose that every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on. Datasheets for datasets will facilitate better communication between dataset creators and dataset consumers, and encourage the machine learning community to prioritize transparency and accountability.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning Practitioners' Data Documentation Perceptions, Needs, Challenges, and Desiderata
resources.abstract: Data is central to the development and evaluation of machine learning (ML) models. However, the use of problematic or inappropriate datasets can result in harms when the resulting models are deployed. To encourage responsible AI practice through more deliberate reflection on datasets and transparency around the processes by which they are created, researchers and practitioners have begun to advocate for increased data documentation and have proposed several data documentation frameworks. However, there is little research on whether these data documentation frameworks meet the needs of ML practitioners, who both create and consume datasets. To address this gap, we set out to understand ML practitioners' data documentation perceptions, needs, challenges, and desiderata, with the goal of deriving design requirements that can inform future data documentation frameworks. We conducted a series of semi-structured interviews with 14 ML practitioners at a single large, international technology company. We had them answer a list of questions taken from datasheets for datasets (Gebru, 2021). Our findings show that current approaches to data documentation are largely ad hoc and myopic in nature. Participants expressed needs for data documentation frameworks to be adaptable to their contexts, integrated into their existing tools and workflows, and automated wherever possible. Despite the fact that data documentation frameworks are often motivated from the perspective of responsible AI, participants did not make the connection between the questions that they were asked to answer and their responsible AI implications. In addition, participants often had difficulties prioritizing the needs of dataset consumers and providing information that someone unfamiliar with their datasets might need to know. Based on these findings, we derive seven design requirements for future data documentation frameworks.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets help ML Engineers Notice and Understand Ethical Issues in Training Data
resources.abstract: The social computing community has demonstrated interest in the ethical issues sometimes produced by machine learning (ML) models, like violations of privacy, fairness, and accountability. This paper discovers what kinds of ethical considerations machine learning engineers recognize, how they build understanding, and what decisions they make when working with a real-world dataset. In particular, it illustrates ways in which Datasheets for Datasets, an accountability intervention designed to help engineers explore unfamiliar training data, scaffolds the process of issue discovery, understanding, and ethical decision-making. Participants were asked to review an intentionally ethically problematic dataset and asked to think aloud as they used it to solve a given ML problem. Out of 23 participants, 11 were given a Datasheet they could use while completing the task. Participants were ethically sensitive enough to identify concerns in the dataset; participants who had a Datasheet did open and refer to it; and those with Datasheets mentioned ethical issues during the think-aloud earlier and more often than than those without. The think-aloud protocol offered a grounded description of how participants recognized, understood, and made a decision about ethical problems in an unfamiliar dataset. The method used in this study can test other interventions that claim to encourage recognition, promote understanding, and support decision-making among technologists.

The dataset's composition by demographic group and its sampling method are documented, so model developers can judge whether the data represents the population the model will serve.

techniques.name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
techniques.description: MLflow Tracking is the part of the open-source MLflow platform that records each run of a machine learning training script. Developers add logging calls to their code, or switch on automatic logging for supported libraries. Each run's record holds its parameters (the settings chosen, including hyperparameters, which are fixed before training), its metrics (results such as accuracy), the code version, its start and end times, and output files called artefacts, such as the trained model. Runs are grouped into experiments that can be searched and compared in a web interface, and they stay on the developer's machine unless a shared tracking server is set up. The result is a dated record of how each model was built, which a reviewer can use to see what was tried and which run produced the deployed model, but only for what was actually logged.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group develops a diagnostic imaging model across three sites. Ahead of an external assessment, the team exports the logged runs, with the parameters, evaluation metrics, code version and time of each run, so the assessor can see every configuration tried and trace the submitted model to the run that produced it.

A bank's fraud-detection team sees alert precision fall after a retraining. They compare the logged runs for the old and new model, covering parameters, training-dataset reference, code version and metrics, find that a feature setting changed, and note the cause on the run before the next release.

An energy company's data science team keeps every hyperparameter search for its demand-forecasting models on a shared tracking server. When an internal auditor asks why one configuration went live, the team shows the full set of runs searched, their metrics and when each was logged, and the run chosen for deployment.

limitations.description: The record holds only what developers log, plus the default set that automatic logging picks up for supported libraries. A preprocessing choice made in a notebook and never logged is absent, and the log gives no sign that anything is missing, so the audit trail is only as complete as the team's logging habits.

Dataset tracking stores metadata about a dataset, such as its name, a hash of its contents and where it came from, not the data itself. A logged run can show which dataset was used but cannot restore it, so reproducing a result needs the data to be versioned or retained separately.

A tracking server is a working store, not a sealed ledger. Runs can be marked as deleted and tags overwritten by anyone with write access, so the log supports an audit only if access is restricted and the store is backed up.

Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively. Where that is not done, the record of one stage will not show what fed it.

Artefact storage grows with every logged model and file, so heavy experimentation with large models raises storage costs. Deleting old runs to save space removes part of the record that an audit would rely on.

resources.title: Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow
resources.abstract: Machine learning development creates multiple new challenges that are not present in a traditional software development lifecycle. These include keeping track of the myriad inputs to an ML application (e.g., data versions, code and tuning parameters), reproducing results, and production deployment. In this paper, we summarize these challenges from our experience with Databricks customers, and describe MLflow, an open source platform we recently launched to streamline the machine learning lifecycle. MLflow covers three key challenges: experimentation, reproducibility, and model deployment, using generic APIs that work with any ML library, algorithm and programming language. The project has a rapidly growing open source community, with over 50 contributors since its launch in June 2018.

An MLOps Framework for Explainable Network Intrusion Detection with MLflow
resources.abstract: The surge in network traffic has required advanced techniques to ensure network security. Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs), which increasingly employ Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methodologies, play a pivotal role in this task by continuously monitoring network traffic patterns and identifying suspicious activities. To address the complexities of developing ML- and DL-based NIDS, MLOps tools have been designed to optimize model deployment, monitoring, and management in production environments, streamlining model development. These tools enable efficient experimentation, version management, and logging of artifacts for network administrators and data scientists. In this work, we design a framework powered by MLflow to manage the ML pipeline from data handling to results visualization. To show the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted an experimental campaign on 4 broadly used security datasets (viz. NSL-KDD, IoT-23, Kitsune, and TON_IoT) performing crucial tasks for intrusion detection, namely anomaly detection, binary misuse detection, and multiclass misuse detection.

resources.title: Enhancing Quantum Software Development Process with Experiment Tracking
resources.abstract: As quantum computing advances from theoretical promise to experimental reality, the need for rigorous experiment tracking becomes critical. Drawing inspiration from best practices in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), we argue that reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration in quantum research can benefit significantly from structured tracking workflows. This paper explores the application of MLflow in quantum research, illustrating how it enables better development practices, experiment reproducibility, decision making, and cross-domain integration in an increasingly hybrid classical-quantum landscape.

techniques.name: Data Version Control
techniques.description: Data Version Control (DVC) is an open-source tool that records which version of a dataset or model was used at each point in a machine learning project. It works alongside Git, the standard system for tracking changes to code. DVC keeps large data and model files in separate storage, such as a cloud storage service, and puts a small pointer file into Git that holds a fingerprint (hash) of the file's contents. A team can also describe a pipeline, meaning the ordered steps from raw data through preprocessing to a trained model, and DVC then records fingerprints of each step's inputs, settings and outputs. Committed to Git, these files give a dated history of how data and models changed and let the team restore an earlier version, but only for what was added to DVC and committed.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a chest X-ray classifier. When a regulator asks which images and preprocessing produced the version it submitted, the group checks out the tagged Git commit, shows the dataset fingerprints and pipeline steps recorded in it, and restores that exact data to confirm.

A lender's credit-scoring team sees approval rates shift after a quarterly data refresh. Using DVC with Git, they list the files that changed between the datasets behind the last two model releases, trace the shift to one refresh, and decide whether to revert to the earlier data version.

A flood-forecasting agency versions its river-sensor calibration data and the feature-extraction steps that use it. When a forecast is challenged, an independent reviewer can see from the version history who changed the calibration data and when, and which model release was trained on each version.

A manufacturer's quality team retrains a defect-detection model each month and tags each release in Git with the DVC record of its training images. When a customer reports a missed defect, the team retrieves the exact images behind the model then in use and sees what was added or removed since the previous release.

limitations.description: DVC records only what has been added to it and committed to Git. Data edited outside DVC, or changes that were never committed, leave no trace, and nothing in the history shows what is missing, so the record is only as complete as the team's habits.

Lineage exists only for steps defined as DVC pipeline stages. A study of 56 open-source projects found that 85.7% used only DVC's versioning and tracking feature, so a project that uses DVC may hold no record of how its data was preprocessed or its model trained.

Restoring an earlier model takes more than DVC's files. The code, the software environment and the stored data must all still exist, and the pipeline lock file records commands, file fingerprints and parameter values but not library versions, so a restored pipeline can still give different results.

Scale costs time and storage. A changed data file is stored again as a new copy, and the documentation notes that operations such as pulling become slow with tens of thousands of files, pointing teams that need to branch and merge large datasets in object storage to a different tool.
When several people change the same data files or pipeline, merge conflicts in DVC's tracking files have to be resolved by hand. Without agreed branching rules the history becomes hard to trust.

resources.title: Get Started with DVC
On the Co-evolution of ML Pipelines and Source Code - Empirical Study of DVC Projects
resources.abstract: The growing popularity of machine learning (ML) applications has led to the introduction of software engineering tools such as Data Versioning Control (DVC), MLFlow and Pachyderm that enable versioning ML data, models, pipelines and model evaluation metrics. Since these versioned ML artifacts need to be synchronized not only with each other, but also with the source and test code of the software applications into which the models are integrated, prior findings on co-evolution and coupling between software artifacts might need to be revisited. Hence, in order to understand the degree of coupling between ML-related and other software artifacts, as well as the adoption of ML versioning features, this paper empirically studies the usage of DVC in 391 Github projects, 25 of which in detail. Our results show that more than half of the DVC files in a project are changed at least once every one-tenth of the project's lifetime. Furthermore, we observe a tight coupling between DVC files and other artifacts, with 1/4 pull requests changing source code and 1/2 pull requests changing tests requiring a change to DVC files. As additional evidence of the observed complexity associated with adopting ML-related software engineering tools like DVC, an average of 78% of the studied projects showed a non-constant trend in pipeline complexity.

resources.title: DVC in Open Source ML-development: The Action and the Reaction
resources.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) systems are gaining popularity, reshaping various domains ranging from customer services to software engineering. The effectiveness of ML systems is dependent on the quality of their training data. Therefore, practitioners invest substantial time experimenting with different data, parameters, and models to guarantee the quality of the end system. Prior work highlighted unique challenges of developing ML systems, particularly concerning versioning data and models. Recently, various tools such as DVC and MLFlow have emerged to aid developers in the storage and tracking of data. Despite their growing popularity, very little is known about their usage patterns and impact on open-source software (OSS) systems. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study on 56 GitHub OSS projects that use DVC to understand the DVC usage pattern and the impact of using DVC on the software development process. We found that Versioning and tracking is the most adopted DVC feature, being utilized by all 56 projects and being the only adopted feature in 85.7% of them. Furthermore, we found that DVC has a significant impact on the software development process indicators such as the number of created pull requests (PRs), and the number of bug-fix commits. For instance, our findings showed that DVC causes a peak in the number of commits and PRs at the moment of the adoption, followed by a long-term decrease. We believe that our findings can assist practitioners in tailoring tools to better meet user requirements and help organizations realize potential outcomes of adopting such tools.

techniques.name: Equal Opportunity Difference
techniques.description: Equal Opportunity Difference checks whether a model is equally likely to give a favourable prediction to the people whose true outcome is favourable, such as loan applicants who would repay, in each demographic group. For each group it calculates the true positive rate: of the people whose true outcome is positive, the share the model also predicts as positive. The score is the gap between two groups' rates, usually the unprivileged group's minus the privileged group's, and 0 means the rates match. Some libraries report the largest gap across all groups instead. The metric follows the equality of opportunity criterion of Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016), and it says nothing about people whose true outcome is negative, so a score of 0 does not show that the model is fair overall.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model risk team evaluates a loan approval model on past loans with known repayment outcomes. It measures whether applicants who went on to repay were approved at the same rate in each ethnic group, for example 90% for one group against a markedly lower rate for another, before the model is released.

A hospital evaluating a model that flags chest X-rays for suspected pneumonia compares its sensitivity, the share of confirmed cases it flags, between male and female patients and between age bands on a labelled validation set. A gap means affected patients in one group are more likely to be missed, which the clinical safety board weighs before deployment.

A university department checks a model that flags first-year students at risk of dropping out so they can be offered support. Using last year's records, it measures what share of students who actually dropped out were flagged, separately for students who are the first in their family to attend university and for other students.

limitations.description: Only considers true positive rates and ignores false positive rate disparities, potentially allowing discrimination in the form of unequal false alarm rates between groups.

The true outcome labels must be reliable for every group. Where they record past decisions, such as repayment known only for applicants previously approved, or are measured differently between groups, equal true positive rates can reproduce the bias already in the labels.

True positive rates use only the people whose true outcome is positive, so a rare outcome leaves few cases in each group. Gaps can then be noise, and splitting by several attributes at once, such as age within gender, makes this worse.

Closing a gap by lowering one group's decision threshold raises that group's true positive rate but also its false positive rate. Fixing this metric can therefore open a gap in another, and the metric gives no warning when it does.

A score of 0 does not show that the model is fair. The measure uses only predictions, true outcomes and group membership, and Hardt et al. show that situations with different fairness readings can give identical numbers, so a result needs scrutiny of how the outcome was produced.

resources.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
resources.abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.   In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individualfeatures. We study the inherent limits of defining and identifying biases based on such oblivious measures, outlining what can and cannot be inferred from different oblivious tests.   We illustrate our notion using a case study of FICO credit scores.

resources.title: AI Fairness 360: An extensible toolkit for detecting and mitigating algorithmic bias
resources.abstract: Fairness is an increasingly important concern as machine learning models are used to support decision making in high-stakes applications such as mortgage lending, hiring, and prison sentencing. This article introduces a new open-source Python toolkit for algorithmic fairness, AI Fairness 360 (AIF360), released under an Apache v2.0 license (https://github.com/ibm/aif360). The main objectives of this toolkit are to help facilitate the transition of fairness research algorithms for use in an industrial setting and to provide a common framework for fairness researchers to share and evaluate algorithms. The package includes a comprehensive set of fairness metrics for datasets and models, explanations for these metrics, and algorithms to mitigate bias in datasets and models. It also includes an interactive Web experience that provides a gentle introduction to the concepts and capabilities for line-of-business users, researchers, and developers to extend the toolkit with their new algorithms and improvements and to use it for performance benchmarking. A built-in testing infrastructure maintains code quality.

resources.title: AIF360 tutorial: Medical Expenditure (notebook)
Identifying and mitigating algorithmic bias in the safety net
resources.abstract: Algorithmic bias occurs when predictive model performance varies meaningfully across sociodemographic classes, exacerbating systemic healthcare disparities. NYC Health + Hospitals, an urban safety net system, assessed bias in two binary classification models in our electronic medical record: one predicting acute visits for asthma and one predicting unplanned readmissions. We evaluated differences in subgroup performance across race/ethnicity, sex, language, and insurance using equal opportunity difference (EOD), a metric comparing false negative rates. The most biased classes (race/ethnicity for asthma, insurance for readmission) were targeted for mitigation using threshold adjustment, which adjusts subgroup thresholds to minimize EOD, and reject option classification, which re-classifies scores near the threshold by subgroup. Successful mitigation was defined as 1) absolute subgroup EODs <5 percentage points, 2) accuracy reduction <10%, and 3) alert rate change <20%. Threshold adjustment met these criteria; reject option classification did not. We introduce a Supplementary Playbook outlining our approach for low-resource bias mitigation.

resources.title: Evaluating algorithmic fairness in the performance of the AHA PREVENT equations versus pooled cohort equations among single-race and multiracial populations
resources.abstract: Background: The performance of AHA PREVENT equation among multiracial individuals has not been assessed. Objective: To assess model performance and fairness of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease) Equation versus Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) among single-race and disaggregated multiracial individuals. Method: This is a retrospective cohort data analysis using electronic health record from a 2010-2023 primary care population in a large integrated healthcare system in California. Patient population was restricted to those who are eligible for both the AHA PREVENT base equation and PCE. The primary outcomes were incident ASCVD based on diagnosis codes. We compared measures of model performance as well as algorithmic fairness between PCE and AHA PREVENT, using Disparate Impact (DI), Average Odds Difference (AOD), and Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD). Results: A total of 298,276 patients aged 40-79 years were included, with an average follow-up time of 8 years (SD=3), of which 9% (N=26,761) self-identified as multiracial. In aggregate, 3.9% of multiracial patients developed ASCVD, ranging from 2.9% (Multiple Asian) to 5.4% (Multiracial American Indian/Alaska Native), compared to 4.4% of all single-race patients. Discriminatory performance of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was good for aggregated multiracial groups (AUC=0.747), ranging from 0.692 (Multiracial Black) to 0.793 (Multiracial Pacific Islander), and was comparable to single-race groups (AUC=0.753). Calibration was generally good among most multiracial groups. However, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was fairer in its predictive ability when compared to the PCE for all three fairness metrics. Conclusions and relevance: With good discriminatory ability and calibration for single race and multiracial groups, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation provides both more accurate and fairer estimates of ASCVD risk compared to PCE.

techniques.name: Average Odds Difference
techniques.description: Average Odds Difference summarises how differently a model treats two demographic groups, using two error rates. The true positive rate is the share of people whose true outcome is positive whom the model also predicts as positive. The false positive rate is the share of people whose true outcome is negative whom the model wrongly predicts as positive. The score is the mean of the gap in each rate between the groups, usually the unprivileged group minus the privileged group, so 0 means the two gaps are absent or cancel out. Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016) call the stricter requirement that both gaps are zero equalised odds, and a score near 0 does not guarantee it.

example_use_cases.description: A court-services analytics team audits a pre-trial risk tool on past cases with known outcomes. It reports the average odds difference between racial groups together with the two gaps it averages: how often defendants who later reoffended were rated high risk, and how often those who did not were wrongly rated high risk. The findings go to the oversight board that decides whether the tool stays in use.

A recruitment firm audits its CV-screening tool on past applications whose suitability hiring managers later confirmed. For men and women it compares how often suitable applicants were advanced and how often unsuitable applicants were advanced, and it tracks the average of the two gaps each quarter to decide whether the tool needs retraining.

A hospital compares a sepsis early-warning model across patient ethnic groups before rollout. It checks the share of true sepsis cases flagged and the share of non-sepsis patients falsely flagged, since missed cases and false alarms both carry costs, and uses the average gap to rank candidate models.

limitations.description: Averaging effect can mask important disparities when false positive and true positive rate differences compensate for each other, potentially hiding significant bias in one direction.

The rates are only as trustworthy as the outcome labels, which can differ in quality between groups. Where outcomes are recorded only for people previously approved or hired, such as repayment for granted loans, the gaps describe a selected subset rather than the whole applicant pool. The sensitive attribute must also be available and lawful to use.

When groups differ in how many members truly have the positive outcome, equal error rates generally cannot be achieved together with scores that mean the same thing in every group (Hardt et al. discuss this result of Kleinberg et al.). Pushing the metric towards 0 can therefore leave a risk score less well calibrated for one group, a trade-off the metric does not weigh.

A score of 0 does not show that the model is fair. The measure uses only predictions, true outcomes and group membership, and Hardt et al. show that situations with very different fairness readings can give identical numbers, so any result needs scrutiny of how the outcome was produced.

Closing the gaps can mean degrading the better-served group instead of improving the other. Hardt et al. show that a predictor meeting equalised odds is only as good as the weakest group's performance, so reaching a score of 0 this way can cost accuracy for everyone.

resources.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
resources.abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.   In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individualfeatures. We study the inherent limits of defining and identifying biases based on such oblivious measures, outlining what can and cannot be inferred from different oblivious tests.   We illustrate our notion using a case study of FICO credit scores.

resources.title: AI Fairness 360: An extensible toolkit for detecting and mitigating algorithmic bias
resources.abstract: Fairness is an increasingly important concern as machine learning models are used to support decision making in high-stakes applications such as mortgage lending, hiring, and prison sentencing. This article introduces a new open-source Python toolkit for algorithmic fairness, AI Fairness 360 (AIF360), released under an Apache v2.0 license (https://github.com/ibm/aif360). The main objectives of this toolkit are to help facilitate the transition of fairness research algorithms for use in an industrial setting and to provide a common framework for fairness researchers to share and evaluate algorithms. The package includes a comprehensive set of fairness metrics for datasets and models, explanations for these metrics, and algorithms to mitigate bias in datasets and models. It also includes an interactive Web experience that provides a gentle introduction to the concepts and capabilities for line-of-business users, researchers, and developers to extend the toolkit with their new algorithms and improvements and to use it for performance benchmarking. A built-in testing infrastructure maintains code quality.

Evaluating algorithmic fairness in the performance of the AHA PREVENT equations versus pooled cohort equations among single-race and multiracial populations
resources.abstract: Background: The performance of AHA PREVENT equation among multiracial individuals has not been assessed. Objective: To assess model performance and fairness of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease) Equation versus Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) among single-race and disaggregated multiracial individuals. Method: This is a retrospective cohort data analysis using electronic health record from a 2010-2023 primary care population in a large integrated healthcare system in California. Patient population was restricted to those who are eligible for both the AHA PREVENT base equation and PCE. The primary outcomes were incident ASCVD based on diagnosis codes. We compared measures of model performance as well as algorithmic fairness between PCE and AHA PREVENT, using Disparate Impact (DI), Average Odds Difference (AOD), and Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD). Results: A total of 298,276 patients aged 40-79 years were included, with an average follow-up time of 8 years (SD=3), of which 9% (N=26,761) self-identified as multiracial. In aggregate, 3.9% of multiracial patients developed ASCVD, ranging from 2.9% (Multiple Asian) to 5.4% (Multiracial American Indian/Alaska Native), compared to 4.4% of all single-race patients. Discriminatory performance of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was good for aggregated multiracial groups (AUC=0.747), ranging from 0.692 (Multiracial Black) to 0.793 (Multiracial Pacific Islander), and was comparable to single-race groups (AUC=0.753). Calibration was generally good among most multiracial groups. However, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was fairer in its predictive ability when compared to the PCE for all three fairness metrics. Conclusions and relevance: With good discriminatory ability and calibration for single race and multiracial groups, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation provides both more accurate and fairer estimates of ASCVD risk compared to PCE.

resources.title: Machine learning evaluation of pneumonia severity: subgroup performance in the Medical Imaging and Data Resource Center modified radiographic assessment of lung edema mastermind challenge
resources.abstract: PurposeThe Medical Imaging and Data Resource Center Mastermind Grand Challenge of modified radiographic assessment of lung edema (mRALE) tasked participants with developing machine learning techniques for automated COVID-19 severity assessment via mRALE scores on portable chest radiographs (CXRs). We examine potential biases across demographic subgroups for the best-performing models of the nine teams participating in the test phase of the challenge.ApproachModels were evaluated against a nonpublic test set of CXRs (814 patients) annotated by radiologists for disease severity (mRALE score 0 to 24). Participants used a variety of data and methods for training. Performance was measured using quadratic-weighted kappa (QWK). Bias analyses considered demographics (sex, age, race, ethnicity, and their intersections) using QWK. In addition, for distinguishing no/mild versus moderate/severe disease, equal opportunity difference (EOD) and average absolute odds difference (AAOD) were calculated. Bias was defined as statistically significant QWK subgroup differences, or EOD outside [−0.1; 0.1], or AAOD outside [0; 0.1].ResultsThe nine models demonstrated good agreement with the reference standard (QWK 0.74 to 0.88). The winning model (QWK = 0.884 [0.819; 0.949]) was the only model without biases identified in terms of QWK. The runner-up model (QWK = 0.874 [0.813; 0.936]) showed no identified biases in terms of EOD and AAOD, whereas the winning model disadvantaged three subgroups in each of these metrics. The median number of disadvantaged subgroups for all models was 3.ConclusionsThe challenge demonstrated strong model performances but identified subgroup disparities. Bias analysis is essential as models with similar accuracy may exhibit varying fairness.

techniques.name: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
techniques.description: Path-specific counterfactual fairness assessment tests whether a protected attribute, such as sex or race, influences a decision along routes that the assessor judges unfair. The assessor first draws a causal graph, a diagram of which variables influence which, and marks each route from the protected attribute to the decision as acceptable or unacceptable. In a classic admissions example, women applied more often to departments with low admission rates, so the effect of sex through department choice was treated as acceptable, while any direct effect of sex was not. The technique then estimates how the decision would change if the protected attribute were switched, counting only the effect that travels along the unacceptable routes. A large estimate points to unfair influence along those routes, and the estimate is only as sound as the graph and the choice of routes.

example_use_cases.description: A company auditing its CV-screening model draws a causal graph from gender to the shortlisting decision. Routes through qualifications are marked acceptable, while the direct route and the route through career-break length are marked unacceptable. The estimated effect along the unacceptable routes tells the audit team whether the model disadvantages women beyond what job-relevant qualifications explain.

A research team auditing ventilation decisions in intensive care uses recorded patient data to estimate how much of the effect of patient race on starting invasive ventilation passes through pulse-oximeter readings, which tend to overstate oxygen levels in dark-skinned patients, and how much through other routes.

limitations.description: Which routes count as unacceptable is a value judgement the assessor must make and defend, and different reasonable choices give different verdicts on the same model. The technique does not settle that question. It only measures the effect along the routes it is given.

The causal graph comes from domain knowledge and cannot be fully checked against observational data. If the graph has a wrong arrow or omits a relevant variable, the assessment can certify an unfair model as compliant, and nothing inside the method flags the error.

Path-specific effects are often not identifiable from observational data alone. When unobserved confounders sit between the protected attribute and the mediating variables or the outcome, the effect along a specific route cannot be uniquely recovered without further parametric assumptions, so the result becomes a bound rather than a point estimate.

Estimating the effect along a route means fitting a model for each variable on it. Outside linear or low-dimensional settings the calculation is hard and relies on approximations, and the answer is only as good as the fitted model's match to the data.
An average effect can hide opposing individual effects. A population-level result does not establish the paper's individual counterfactual criterion for every person.

resources.title: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of learning fair decision systems from data in which a sensitive attribute might affect the decision along both fair and unfair pathways. We introduce a counterfactual approach to disregard effects along unfair pathways that does not incur in the same loss of individual-specific information as previous approaches. Our method corrects observations adversely affected by the sensitive attribute, and uses these to form a decision. We leverage recent developments in deep learning and approximate inference to develop a VAE-type method that is widely applicable to complex nonlinear models.

resources.title: A Causal Framework for Discovering and Removing Direct and Indirect Discrimination
resources.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the problem of discovering both direct and indirect discrimination from the historical data, and removing the discriminatory effects before the data is used for predictive analysis (e.g., building classifiers). The main drawback of existing methods is that they cannot distinguish the part of influence that is really caused by discrimination from all correlated influences. In our approach, we make use of the causal network to capture the causal structure of the data. Then we model direct and indirect discrimination as the path-specific effects, which accurately identify the two types of discrimination as the causal effects transmitted along different paths in the network. Based on that, we propose an effective algorithm for discovering direct and indirect discrimination, as well as an algorithm for precisely removing both types of discrimination while retaining good data utility. Experiments using the real dataset show the effectiveness of our approaches.

resources.title: Causal Fairness Analysis: A Causal Toolkit for Fair Machine Learning
resources.abstract: Decision-making systems based on AI and machine learning have been used throughout a wide range of real-world scenarios, including healthcare, law enforcement, education, and finance. It is no longer far-fetched to envision a future where autonomous systems will drive entire business decisions and, more broadly, support large-scale decision-making infrastructure to solve society’s most challenging problems. Issues of unfairness and discrimination are pervasive when decisions are being made by humans, and remain (or are potentially amplified) when decisions are made using machines with little transparency, accountability, and fairness. In this monograph, we introduce a framework for causal fairness analysis with the intent of filling in this gap, i.e., understanding, modeling, and possibly solving issues of fairness in decision-making settings. The main insight of our approach will be to link the quantification of the disparities present in the observed data with the underlying, often unobserved, collection of causal mechanisms that generate the disparity in the first place, a challenge we call the Fundamental Problem of Causal Fairness Analysis (FPCFA). In order to solve the FPCFA, we study the problem of decomposing variations and empirical measures of fairness that attribute such variations to structural mechanisms and different units of the population. Our effort culminates in the Fairness Map, the first systematic attempt to organize and explain the relationship between various criteria found in the literature. Finally, we study which causal assumptions are minimally needed for performing causal fairness analysis and propose the Fairness Cookbook, which allows one to assess the existence of disparate impact and disparate treatment.

Path-specific effects for pulse-oximetry guided decisions in critical care
resources.abstract: Identifying and measuring biases associated with sensitive attributes is a crucial consideration in healthcare to prevent treatment disparities. One prominent issue is inaccurate pulse oximeter readings, which tend to overestimate oxygen saturation for dark-skinned patients and misrepresent supplemental oxygen needs. Most existing research has revealed statistical disparities linking device measurement errors to patient outcomes in intensive care units (ICUs) without causal formalization. This study causally investigates how racial discrepancies in oximetry measurements affect invasive ventilation in ICU settings. We employ a causal inference-based approach using path-specific effects to isolate the impact of bias by race on clinical decision-making. To estimate these effects, we leverage a doubly robust estimator, propose its self-normalized variant for improved sample efficiency, and provide novel finite-sample guarantees. Our methodology is validated on semi-synthetic data and applied to two large real-world health datasets: MIMIC-IV and eICU. Contrary to prior work, our analysis reveals minimal impact of racial discrepancies on invasive ventilation rates. However, path-specific effects mediated by oxygen saturation disparity are more pronounced on ventilation duration, and the severity differs across datasets. Our work provides a novel pipeline for investigating potential disparities in clinical decision-making and, more importantly, highlights the necessity of causal methods to robustly assess fairness in healthcare.

techniques.name: Embedding Bias Analysis
techniques.description: Embedding bias analysis tests whether the numerical representations a model uses for words, images or documents link social groups to stereotyped attributes. An embedding places each item at a point in a many-dimensional space so that similar items sit close together. The best-known test, the Word Embedding Association Test (Caliskan et al., 2017), compares how close two sets of target words, such as engineering and nursing occupations, sit to two sets of attribute words, such as male and female terms, and reports an effect size and a significance level. Other analyses project embeddings onto a gender or ethnicity direction, or cluster them to see whether groups separate. The scores describe the representation itself, and any link to bias in an application built on it has to be tested separately.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a CV-screening tool must choose between two pretrained word embedding sets. It runs association tests on each, comparing how close male and female terms sit to career and family words, and drops or mitigates the set with the larger stereotyped association before building on it.

Analysing clinical note embeddings in a medical diagnosis support system to detect whether disease associations cluster along demographic lines (for example, certain conditions being systematically closer to particular age or ethnic groups in the embedding space), which could lead to biased treatment recommendations.

Auditing loan application embeddings to detect whether protected characteristics (ethnicity, gender, age) cluster near creditworthiness concepts in ways that could enable indirect discrimination in lending decisions.

limitations.description: Bias found in an embedding space does not reliably predict bias in the systems built on it. Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. (2021) found no consistent correlation between association-test scores and gaps between groups in downstream tasks, so a clean or a biased result here needs a separate test on the application itself.

Results depend on the word or sentence lists chosen to represent each group and attribute. Swapping one published list of pleasant words for another moved the effect size in the original study from 1.50 to 1.28, so a single list can overstate or understate bias, and lists written in one culture or language may not transfer.

A passing score does not show that bias is absent. Tests and projections look only for the pattern they are built to find, and Gonen and Goldberg (2019) showed that gender information removed by projection could still be recovered from the distances between words.

There is no agreed threshold for an acceptable association. An effect size describes how strongly two groups of terms differ in closeness, not how much harm follows, so what counts as a pass depends on the application and has to be set and justified by the team.

Needs the embedding vectors themselves, so it cannot be run on a system that exposes only final decisions or text. Pretrained vectors can be tested without the training data, as the original study did with published GloVe vectors.

resources.title: Semantics derived automatically from language corpora contain human-like biases
resources.abstract: Machines learn what people know implicitly AlphaGo has demonstrated that a machine can learn how to do things that people spend many years of concentrated study learning, and it can rapidly learn how to do them better than any human can. Caliskan et al. now show that machines can learn word associations from written texts and that these associations mirror those learned by humans, as measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT) (see the Perspective by Greenwald). Why does this matter? Because the IAT has predictive value in uncovering the association between concepts, such as pleasantness and flowers or unpleasantness and insects. It can also tease out attitudes and beliefs—for example, associations between female names and family or male names and career. Such biases may not be expressed explicitly, yet they can prove influential in behavior. Science , this issue p. 183 ; see also p. 133

resources.title: Bias Measurement — WEFE user guide
Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

resources.title: Word embeddings quantify 100 years of gender and ethnic stereotypes
resources.abstract: Significance Word embeddings are a popular machine-learning method that represents each English word by a vector, such that the geometry between these vectors captures semantic relations between the corresponding words. We demonstrate that word embeddings can be used as a powerful tool to quantify historical trends and social change. As specific applications, we develop metrics based on word embeddings to characterize how gender stereotypes and attitudes toward ethnic minorities in the United States evolved during the 20th and 21st centuries starting from 1910. Our framework opens up a fruitful intersection between machine learning and quantitative social science.

resources.title: Image Representations Learned With Unsupervised Pre-Training Contain Human-like Biases
resources.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning leverage massive datasets of unlabeled images from the web to learn general-purpose image representations for tasks from image classification to face recognition. But do unsupervised computer vision models automatically learn implicit patterns and embed social biases that could have harmful downstream effects? We develop a novel method for quantifying biased associations between representations of social concepts and attributes in images. We find that state-of-the-art unsupervised models trained on ImageNet, a popular benchmark image dataset curated from internet images, automatically learn racial, gender, and intersectional biases. We replicate 8 previously documented human biases from social psychology, from the innocuous, as with insects and flowers, to the potentially harmful, as with race and gender. Our results closely match three hypotheses about intersectional bias from social psychology. For the first time in unsupervised computer vision, we also quantify implicit human biases about weight, disabilities, and several ethnicities. When compared with statistical patterns in online image datasets, our findings suggest that machine learning models can automatically learn bias from the way people are stereotypically portrayed on the web.

sample_claims.text: Association tests on the embeddings used by the CV-screening tool show no gender association between occupation terms and male or female terms above the effect size the team agreed to act on.

The clinical term embeddings in the diagnosis support model show no association between diagnosis terms and age or ethnicity terms above the agreed threshold, and the result holds with a second set of term lists.
Protected-characteristic terms do not sit systematically closer to creditworthiness terms than to their opposites in the lending model's text embeddings, under the word lists documented in the audit.

techniques.name: Few-Shot Fairness Evaluation
techniques.description: Few-shot fairness evaluation tests whether the worked examples placed in a prompt change how fairly a language model treats different demographic groups. The evaluator builds many versions of the same prompt, varying which examples appear and how each demographic group is represented among them. Each version is run on the same test inputs, and group-level results are compared across versions. Typical checks include the gap in outcomes between groups, whether outputs echo stereotypes present in the examples, and whether an input gets the same treatment when only a demographic term in it is swapped. The result shows how sensitive the model's fairness is to the choice of examples, and which compositions make outcomes more or less even.

example_use_cases.description: Testing whether a resume screening LLM's few-shot examples inadvertently introduce gender bias by showing more male examples for technical positions, affecting how it evaluates subsequent applicants.

Evaluating whether a medical triage LLM's few-shot examples for symptom assessment inadvertently encode demographic biases (e.g., more examples of cardiac symptoms in male patients), leading to differential urgency assessments across patient populations.

Assessing whether few-shot examples in a loan application review assistant systematically present more favourable examples for certain demographic profiles, biasing the model's assessment of creditworthiness for subsequent applications.

Testing whether an automated essay grading system keeps consistent standards across student demographics when its few-shot examples over-represent particular writing styles, dialects or cultural references.

limitations.description: The number of possible example sets, orderings and wordings is far too large to test exhaustively. The evaluation samples configurations and can miss the combinations that cause the worst disparities, so results describe what was tested rather than every prompt the system will meet.

Fairness measures can shift with small changes in example wording, order or prompt format, and with ordinary sampling variation in the model's replies. A gap between two example sets may be noise unless each is run repeatedly, and results seldom carry over to a different prompt template, instruction style or model version.

Needs test inputs labelled with demographic attributes, or pairs of inputs that differ only in a demographic term. These can be unavailable, costly to build or sensitive to hold, and they must reflect how the system will actually be prompted, which takes domain expertise to judge.

Each extra example set multiplies the number of model calls, because every set must be run on enough inputs for each group being compared. With large models and high inference costs, thorough coverage is expensive, which tempts teams to test fewer configurations.

resources.title: Fairness-guided few-shot prompting for large language models
resources.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated surprising ability to perform in-context learning, i.e., these models can be directly applied to solve numerous downstream tasks by conditioning on a prompt constructed by a few input-output examples. However, prior research has shown that in-context learning can suffer from high instability due to variations in training examples, example order, and prompt formats. Therefore, the construction of an appropriate prompt is essential for improving the performance of in-context learning. In this paper, we revisit this problem from the view of predictive bias. Specifically, we introduce a metric to evaluate the predictive bias of a fixed prompt against labels or a given attributes. Then we empirically show that prompts with higher bias always lead to unsatisfactory predictive quality. Based on this observation, we propose a novel search strategy based on the greedy search to identify the near-optimal prompt for improving the performance of in-context learning. We perform comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art mainstream models such as GPT-3 on various downstream tasks. Our results indicate that our method can enhance the model's in-context learning performance in an effective and interpretable manner.

resources.title: Strategic Demonstration Selection for Improved Fairness in LLM In-Context Learning
resources.abstract: Recent studies highlight the effectiveness of using in-context learning (ICL) to steer large language models (LLMs) in processing tabular data, a challenging task given the structured nature of such data.Despite advancements in performance, the fairness implications of these methods are less understood.This study investigates how varying demonstrations within ICL prompts influence the fairness outcomes of LLMs.Our findings reveal that deliberately including minority group samples in prompts significantly boosts fairness without sacrificing predictive accuracy.Further experiments demonstrate that the proportion of minority to majority samples in demonstrations affects the trade-off between fairness and prediction accuracy.Based on these insights, we introduce a mitigation technique that employs clustering and evolutionary strategies to curate a diverse and representative sample set from the training data.This approach aims to enhance both predictive performance and fairness in ICL applications.Experimental results validate that our proposed method dramatically improves fairness across various metrics, showing its efficacy in real-world scenarios.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.
